Title: The success screen is shown whether or not the registration succeeded
Description and impact: The submit handler neither awaits the response nor handles a rejection: the service call and the navigation to the thank-you screen sit one after another. The user believes an account was created when none exists. This defect masks every other registration failure, so it has to be fixed before the rest.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the registration form.
2. Fill every field with valid values, entering password1 in both password fields.
3. Tick the consent checkbox and press S'inscrire.
4. Open the network panel and inspect the response to POST /users/create.
5. Run select count(*) from users against the database.
Actual result: The server returned 400 Bad Request, the console shows Uncaught (in promise) AxiosError, the users table holds zero rows. The screen reads “Thank you for subscription!”.
Expected result: The user stays on the form, sees an error message and can correct the data.
How to fix: Await the promise, navigate to /success only on the success branch, surface the error inside the form. The same behaviour reproduces with the backend container fully stopped: ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED, success screen.

Title: An id field in the request body overwrites an existing user
Description and impact: TypeORM's save() performs an upsert: when the incoming object carries a primary key, the row is updated instead of inserted. The body is not filtered at all, so an unauthenticated request silently replaces any user's data. This is data loss and account takeover in a single command.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Create a user with an ordinary request and note its id, for example 2.
2. Send POST /users/create with "id": 2 added to the body, plus a different name, email and phone.
3. Read the row with id = 2 from the users table.
Actual result: The response is 201 Created, yet no row was created: the existing one was overwritten from Jean / a@b.co to ATTACKER / attacker@evil.co.
Expected result: The id field in the body is ignored, a new row is created, existing data is untouched.
How to fix: Enable a global ValidationPipe with whitelist and forbidNonWhitelisted, and replace save() with insert() or build the entity explicitly from allowed fields.

Title: The password is stored in the database in clear text
Description and impact: The password is written to the column as received, with no hashing. Any dump, backup or access to the database port exposes every user's password at once. People reuse passwords, so the damage reaches well beyond this service.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Register a user with the password Abcdef1!.
2. Run select email, password from users.
Actual result: The password column holds the literal string Abcdef1!.
Expected result: An irreversible hash is stored, from which the password cannot be recovered.
How to fix: Hash the password with bcrypt or argon2id before saving, rename the column to password_hash, and treat every existing value as compromised.

Title: The password is written to the application log in clear text
Description and impact: The controller prints the whole request body, password included. The container log flows into whatever log aggregation is in place, where far more people can read it than can read the database. Together with DEF-30 this applies to every environment started from the README.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Confirm that the DEBUG variable is true, as it is by default.
2. Send a registration with the password LogLeak9!.
3. Run docker logs against the backend container and search for the password line.
Actual result: The log prints the full request body: password: 'LogLeak9!' next to the email and phone number.
Expected result: The password never reaches the log under any environment configuration.
How to fix: Mask the password before printing, or log only a request id and the response code.

Title: Client and server describe the password requirements with different rules
Description and impact: Two independent regular expressions impose different requirements. The client asks for a letter and a digit; the server asks for an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a digit and a special character. The two sets of accepted special characters differ as well. Combined with DEF-01 this silently loses a registration on the most ordinary password.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Type the password password1 into the form and confirm the form accepts it.
2. Send the same password directly to POST /users/create.
3. Send the password Abcdef1^ to the API.
4. Type Abcdef1^ into the form.
Actual result: password1: the form accepts it, the API answers 400 “ERROR: invalid password”. Abcdef1^: the API answers 201, the form rejects it.
Expected result: The same value is accepted or rejected identically on both layers.
How to fix: Move the rule into a shared module used by both the form and the server DTO, and derive the error message from that same rule.

Title: The project does not start with the command from the README
Description and impact: Dependency versions are not pinned, so an install pulls whatever is current today. Two of them require Node 20 while docker-compose pins Node 18. The install fails and the application never starts. For a reviewer this means the assignment cannot be run without editing files first.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Clone the repository into a clean directory.
2. Run docker compose up in the project root.
3. Read the output of the backend and frontend containers.
Actual result: Both containers fail during dependency installation: “@nestjs/mapped-types@12.0.0: The engine "node" is incompatible with this module. Expected version ">=20.19.0". Got "18.20.8"”, and the same error for sass@1.104.0.
Expected result: docker compose up brings the application up and it is reachable on port 3000.
How to fix: Commit the lock files, pin @nestjs/mapped-types and sass to compatible versions, or raise the Node image to a supported one. The root cause is DEF-28.

Title: Pressing Backspace in the phone field permanently disables the minimum-length check
Description and impact: The key handler sets the minimum length to zero on any Backspace and never restores it. Deleting a single character is enough for the form to accept a one-digit phone number. A leftover console.log('delete') sits next to it in the code.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Reload the form.
2. Type two digits into the Numéro de téléphone field and confirm the error “Phone Number must be at least 8 characters” appears.
3. Press Backspace once.
4. Type one more digit.
Actual result: The field holds 121 and the minimum-length error is gone. The check never comes back until the page is reloaded.
Expected result: The minimum-length error stays until the field holds at least eight digits.
How to fix: Remove the onKeyDown handler and the minLength state, and set the minimum length as a constant. Remove the debug output while you are there.

Title: A body without a first or last name produces HTTP 500
Description and impact: The emptiness check iterates over the keys of the received object, so fields missing from the body are never seen. There are no dedicated checks for the names either. The request reaches the insert and fails on a NOT NULL constraint, and the client gets “Internal server error” instead of a usable description.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create with a valid last name, email, phone, password and consent, but without the first_name key.
2. Repeat the request, removing last_name instead.
Actual result: Both requests answer 500 with the body {"statusCode":500,"message":"Internal server error"}.
Expected result: 400 naming the field that is missing.
How to fix: Add class-validator and a global ValidationPipe, and mark every DTO field as required.

Title: The email address is not unique — one address registers any number of times
Description and impact: The schema carries no unique index and the service performs no lookup for an existing user. Duplicates make sign-in and password recovery impossible, because an address no longer identifies a single account.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send a registration for dup@example.com.
2. Send exactly the same request a second time.
3. Run select id, email from users where email = 'dup@example.com'.
Actual result: Both requests answer 201 and the table holds two rows with the same address.
Expected result: The second request is rejected with 409 and a message saying the address is taken.
How to fix: Declare the column as @Column({unique: true}), catch the constraint violation and return 409. Lower-case the address before saving.

Title: Nothing prevents the form from being submitted twice
Description and impact: The button is not disabled while the request is in flight and there is no submitting state. Every click issues its own request, and the server does not reject duplicates because the address is not unique either. A user who double-clicks through a slow connection ends up with two accounts.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Empty the users table.
2. Fill the form with valid values.
3. Press the S'inscrire button three times in quick succession.
4. Run select id, email from users.
Actual result: Three requests were sent, all answered 201, and the table holds three identical rows.
Expected result: Exactly one record is created regardless of how many times the button is pressed.
How to fix: Disable the button while formState.isSubmitting is true, and add a unique index on the email column.

Title: A name with diacritics is rejected by a French-language form
Description and impact: The regular expression allows only unaccented Latin letters plus space, comma, full stop, apostrophe and hyphen. The form is entirely in French, yet François, Amélie and Noëlle cannot register. For the target audience this is a plain denial of service. The server accepts the same values, so the two layers disagree.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Type François into the Votre prenom field.
3. Type Amélie.
4. Send François directly to POST /users/create.
Actual result: The form answers “Please enter a valid first name” for both names. The API accepts the same name with 201 and stores it.
Expected result: Names with diacritics are accepted by both layers.
How to fix: Switch to Unicode properties: /^[\p{L}\p{M} ,.'-]+$/u, and mirror the same rule in the server DTO.

Title: The phone field accepts digits only, with no separators
Description and impact: Both the international +33 6 12 34 56 78 and the national 06 12 34 56 78 contain a plus sign and spaces, so both are rejected. These are the two ways a French user writes a phone number by default. The user is left to guess that the separators must be deleted.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Type +33612345678 into the Numéro de téléphone field.
3. Type 06 12 34 56 78.
Actual result: Both values are rejected. The error text reads “Ce champ est requis” even though the field is filled in — see DEF-39.
Expected result: The value is normalised before validation: separators and a country code are accepted.
How to fix: Strip everything but digits and a leading plus before validating, or use libphonenumber.

Title: The maximum name length depends on the user agent string
Description and impact: The rule branches on whether the user agent contains the substring Chrome: the limit is 28 characters in Chrome and 40 everywhere else. The error text says 28 in both cases. Identical data behaves differently for different users, and a bug report cannot be reproduced without knowing the browser.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form in Chrome and type a 30-letter Latin name.
2. Open the same form in a browser whose user agent does not contain Chrome, for example Firefox.
3. Type the same 30 characters.
Actual result: Chrome rejects the value with “First Name must be less than 28 characters”. Firefox accepts the very same value.
Expected result: The limit is identical in every browser and matches the message text.
How to fix: Remove the user-agent branch, move the limit into a constant, and mirror the check on the server.

Title: A hard minimum width on the last-name field breaks the mobile layout
Description and impact: The field carries an inline min-width of 400px. On a 375-pixel screen the field is wider than the viewport and spills past the left edge of the card onto the background. The form looks broken on the most common class of device.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Set the window width to 375 pixels or enable mobile device emulation.
3. Inspect the Votre nom field.
Actual result: The field measures 400 pixels while its neighbours measure 275. Its left edge sits off-screen and its right edge at 325 pixels.
Expected result: Every field in the form shares a width and fits inside the card.
How to fix: Remove the inline minWidth style.

Title: The server does not limit the length of the first or last name
Description and impact: Server-side validation covers consent, phone, password and email. For the first and last name there is neither a length check nor a character-set check. Together with DEF-27 a string of arbitrary size reaches the database, bounded only by the request body limit.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create where first_name consists of 10,000 A characters.
2. Read the stored row from the table.
Actual result: The response is 201 and the value is stored in full, all 10,000 characters.
Expected result: 400 stating the permitted length.
How to fix: Add @Length to the DTO and constrain the column length in the schema.

Title: The server does not limit the phone number length
Description and impact: The server rule only checks that the string consists of digits. There is no minimum and no maximum, so a one-digit number is stored. The client-side bounds of 8 and 16 live in the form alone and are bypassed by a direct API call or by defect DEF-07.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create with phone_number set to 7.
2. Read the stored row.
Actual result: The response is 201 and the database holds the phone number 7, one character long.
Expected result: 400: the number is shorter than the minimum permitted length.
How to fix: Move the length bounds into the server DTO and keep them in step with the form.

Title: The server sets no upper bound on password length
Description and impact: The server expression ends with an unbounded quantifier, so password length is limited only by the request body size. The client, meanwhile, caps the password at 28 characters. Beyond the mismatch between layers, this loads whatever hashing algorithm is adopted later.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create with a 1000-character password that satisfies the server rule.
2. Check the response code.
Actual result: The response is 201 and the password is stored in full.
Expected result: 400: the password exceeds the permitted 28 characters.
How to fix: Add an upper bound to the server rule and keep it equal to the client's.

Title: Unknown fields in the request body are accepted and echoed back
Description and impact: There is no global ValidationPipe and the DTOs are plain classes without decorators, so the body is never filtered. Any extra field passes through the service and into the response. That same absence of filtering is what makes DEF-02 possible.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create with "role": "admin" added to the body.
2. Read the response body.
Actual result: The response is 201 and its body contains {"role":"admin", ...}.
Expected result: The field is dropped, or the request is rejected with 400.
How to fix: app.useGlobalPipes(new ValidationPipe({whitelist: true, forbidNonWhitelisted: true})) plus class-validator decorators on every DTO field.

Title: Consent is accepted for any truthy value
Description and impact: The check tests the field for truthiness rather than for equality with true. The string "false" is truthy in JavaScript, so it counts as consent. The field is legally meaningful — it records acceptance of the terms of use — and it is effectively unchecked.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create with "is_agree": "false".
2. Repeat the request with "is_agree": 1.
3. Repeat it with "is_agree": "no".
Actual result: All three requests answer 201 and create a user.
Expected result: 400 for any value other than the boolean true.
How to fix: An @IsBoolean decorator in the DTO and a strict comparison against true.

Title: Value types in the request body are not validated
Description and impact: The DTO fields are declared as strings but carry no validation decorators, so anything at all lands in them. A number and an array reach the data layer and are coerced to text on write, leaving values such as {"a","b"} in the database.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create with "first_name": 12345.
2. Repeat it with "first_name": ["a","b"].
3. Read the stored rows.
Actual result: Both requests answer 201. The database holds the strings 12345 and {"a","b"}.
Expected result: 400: the field must be a string.
How to fix: @IsString and @IsNotEmpty on the string fields of the DTO.

Title: The database volume is mounted at a path Postgres never uses
Description and impact: The dbdata volume is mounted at /var/lib/mysql while Postgres keeps its data in /var/lib/postgresql/data. The real data lives in the container's writable layer and is destroyed by docker compose down. Every registered user disappears without warning, and the volume itself stays permanently empty.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Register a user and confirm the row appears in the table.
2. Run docker compose down.
3. Run docker compose up -d.
4. Read the users table.
Actual result: The table is empty. Inside the container /var/lib/postgresql/data occupies 40 MB while the mounted /var/lib/mysql holds no files at all.
Expected result: Registered users survive a restart of the stack.
How to fix: Mount the volume at /var/lib/postgresql/data.

Title: Registration is not rate-limited
Description and impact: The endpoint is open, there is no rate limiter, and there is no address confirmation or captcha either. The table can be filled with an arbitrary number of records in seconds, and once outbound email exists the service becomes a tool for mailing strangers.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send sixty POST /users/create requests in a row with different addresses.
2. Inspect the response codes and the elapsed time.
Actual result: Sixty 201 responses in 0.94 seconds, with no rejections.
Expected result: After a handful of consecutive requests the service answers 429 Too Many Requests.
How to fix: Add @nestjs/throttler to the endpoint and a captcha to the form.

Title: The root controller is not registered with the application module
Description and impact: AppController and AppService exist and return the string “Service is working!”, but neither appears in the module's controller list. The GET / route is never registered, so there is no liveness check, and the project's own e2e test targets precisely that route.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Start the backend.
2. Send a GET request to the service root.
Actual result: The response is 404 Not Found.
Expected result: 200 with the body “Service is working!”, as declared in the code and in test/app.e2e-spec.ts.
How to fix: Add AppController to controllers and AppService to providers in the module.

Title: The bundled e2e test cannot run because of an unresolvable import
Description and impact: The service imports a module at the path src/config/regex.config, which resolves through baseUrl during a Nest build but is not configured in the Jest e2e config. The suite fails at module resolution, no test executes, and the command exits with an error.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Install the backend dependencies.
2. Run yarn test:e2e.
Actual result: Cannot find module 'src/config/regex.config' from 'user/user.service.ts'. Test Suites: 1 failed, Tests: 0 total.
Expected result: The test runs and reports the result of its assertion.
How to fix: Add moduleNameMapper or modulePaths to test/jest-e2e.json, or change the import to a relative path.

Title: The unit test command fails because there are no tests
Description and impact: The project contains no spec files at all, and Jest is configured to treat an empty match set as an error. The test step of any pipeline will be permanently red, and the exit code cannot distinguish “no tests” from “tests failed”.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Install the backend dependencies.
2. Run yarn test.
Actual result: testRegex: .*\.spec\.ts$ — 0 matches, and the command exits with code 1.
Expected result: Tests exist and pass, or the step is explicitly marked as skipped.
How to fix: Add unit tests for at least UserService.validateData, where all the business logic sits.

Title: None of the form fields has an accessible name
Description and impact: Field captions are drawn as separate blocks beside the inputs and are not associated with them in any way. The page contains no label element, no id and no aria-label. The component consumes the placeholder prop to render the caption, so the inputs carry no placeholder attribute either. A screen reader user hears seven unnamed text fields in a row.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Run document.querySelectorAll('label').length in the console.
3. Check the inputs for id, aria-label and placeholder attributes.
4. Walk through the form with a screen reader enabled.
Actual result: There are 0 label elements, 0 inputs with an id, 0 with aria-label and 0 with a placeholder attribute. The screen reader announces the fields without names.
Expected result: Every field has an accessible name matching its visible caption.
How to fix: Wrap the caption in a label with a for attribute and give the inputs ids, or pass aria-label.

Title: The text columns are declared without a length limit
Description and impact: All five text columns are typed character varying with no length, so they accept a string of any size. Together with DEF-15 this means a record is bounded only by the HTTP body limit, and a single registration can occupy tens of kilobytes.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Start the database.
2. Run \d users in psql.
3. Inspect the character_maximum_length column in information_schema.columns.
Actual result: Five character varying columns, every one of them with character_maximum_length set to NULL.
Expected result: Each text column carries a sensible maximum length.
How to fix: Set length in the @Column decorators and apply the change through a migration.

Title: Lock files are excluded from the repository
Description and impact: yarn.lock is listed in .gitignore, so the dependency tree is recomputed on every install. The build stops being reproducible: two developers and the pipeline end up with different versions, and over time the project breaks on its own. That is exactly what happened — see DEF-06.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open .gitignore in the repository root.
2. Find the yarn.lock entry.
3. Install dependencies twice with a gap between and compare the resolved versions.
Actual result: yarn.lock is listed in .gitignore and no lock file is present in the repository.
Expected result: Lock files are committed and installs are reproducible.
How to fix: Remove yarn.lock from .gitignore and commit it for both packages.

Title: Markup is stored in the database unescaped and unrejected
Description and impact: A value containing a script tag is written verbatim. There is no direct exploit today because no endpoint reads the data back, but the first admin screen or the first email carrying a user's name turns this into stored cross-site scripting. The defect is latent, and fixing it now is cheaper.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create where first_name contains a script tag calling alert.
2. Read the stored value from the database.
Actual result: The response is 201 and the value is stored verbatim, angle brackets included.
Expected result: The value is rejected by a character-set check or escaped on write.
How to fix: Restrict the permitted character set in the DTO and escape values wherever they are rendered.

Title: Debug output is enabled by default in the run configuration
Description and impact: The DEBUG variable defaults to true inside docker-compose itself. That means every environment started from the README prints request bodies along with passwords. This defect turns DEF-04 from a possible problem into an actual one.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open docker-compose.yml and find the DEBUG variable line.
2. Start the stack with the README command, setting no environment variables.
3. Send a registration and read the container log.
Actual result: DEBUG: ${DEBUG:-true} — the default is true and request bodies are printed.
Expected result: The default is false and debug output is switched on deliberately.
How to fix: Change the default to false and move the variables into a .env file.

Title: Cross-origin access is granted to any site
Description and impact: Calling enableCors with no options returns a wildcard header, so any page on the internet can submit a registration on behalf of whoever opened it. With no captcha and no rate limit this is a ready-made channel for inflating sign-ups.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send OPTIONS to /users/create with the header Origin: https://evil.example.
2. Send a POST to the same path with the same Origin header.
3. Inspect the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header in both responses.
Actual result: The preflight answers 204 and the main request 201, both carrying Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.
Expected result: Only the application's own frontend origin is allowed.
How to fix: Pass an explicit list of allowed origins from configuration into enableCors.

Title: The HTTP client has no timeout configured
Description and impact: The axios instance is created without a timeout, so a request to a host that accepts the connection but never answers hangs until the operating system gives up. On its own that is a stuck request; combined with DEF-01 the user is already on the success screen and never learns anything went wrong.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the axios configuration in frontend/src/api/interceptors.ts.
2. Confirm that no timeout option is set.
3. Submit the form against a host that accepts the connection but does not respond.
Actual result: No timeout option is present and the request stays pending indefinitely.
Expected result: The request aborts after a sensible interval and the user sees a timeout message.
How to fix: Set timeout on the axios instance configuration and handle the ECONNABORTED error code.

Title: The database port is published on every network interface
Description and impact: Port 5432 is bound to 0.0.0.0, so the database is reachable from the local network. Together with the password from DEF-70 and clear-text password storage from DEF-03, this means a stranger on any untrusted network reads every user's password. The application does not need external access: the services talk over the internal Docker network.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Start the stack.
2. Run docker compose ps and inspect the ports column.
3. Try connecting to port 5432 from another machine on the same network.
Actual result: 0.0.0.0:5432->5432/tcp — the database accepts connections from any address.
Expected result: The database port is not published at all, or is bound to 127.0.0.1.
How to fix: Drop the port mapping from the db service; for debugging use a 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 binding.

Title: The password error text describes a rule that does not exist
Description and impact: The message demands an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter and a digit, while the expression only checks for any letter and a digit. The special-character requirement enforced by the server is not mentioned at all. The user picks a password from an incorrect hint and is rejected by the server anyway.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Type password1 into the password field — it has no uppercase letter.
2. Type 27 uppercase letters followed by a digit — it has no lowercase letter.
3. Read the error text shown for an invalid password.
Actual result: Both values are accepted by the form, even though the message reads “Minimum eight characters, at least one uppercase letter, one lowercase letter and one number”.
Expected result: The message describes the rule that is actually applied, special character included.
How to fix: Generate the text from the shared rule introduced when fixing DEF-05.
Covering cases: TC-FV-053 TC-FV-055 TC-FV-056 TC-FV-057 TC-FV-059 TC-FV-072

Title: The maximum-length messages are off by one
Description and impact: The wording “less than N” is used where exactly N is allowed. The mistake repeats across four fields: first name, last name, phone and both password fields. It is small, but it consistently misleads anyone probing boundary values and reads as carelessness.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Type exactly 28 characters into the first-name field.
2. Type 29 characters and read the error text.
3. Repeat for the phone field with 16 and then 17 digits.
Actual result: 28 characters is accepted; at 29 the message reads “First Name must be less than 28 characters”. 16 digits is accepted; at 17 it reads “Phone Number must be less than 16 characters”.
Expected result: The text matches the boundary: “no more than 28 characters”.
How to fix: Correct the wording in all four fields.

Title: The last-name error message talks about the first name
Description and impact: The first-name message was copied into the rule for the Votre nom field. A user seeing the error looks for the problem in the wrong field.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Type a value with a disallowed character, such as François, into the Votre nom field.
3. Read the error text below the field.
Actual result: “Please enter a valid first name” is shown beneath the last-name field.
Expected result: The message refers to the last name.
How to fix: Correct the text to say last name.

Title: A four-character minimum on the name rejects real names
Description and impact: Luc, Ali, Bo and Ève are ordinary two- and three-letter names, several of them common in France. A four-character minimum follows neither from the domain nor from any database constraint, and simply turns some users away.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Type Luc into the Votre prenom field.
Actual result: “First Name must be at least 4 characters” is shown and the value is rejected.
Expected result: A two- or three-character name is accepted.
How to fix: Lower the minimum to one character and keep the character-set check.

Title: Typo in the confirm-password field caption
Description and impact: It reads “Confirmez vorte mot de passe” instead of “votre”. The typo is visible on the first screen and undermines the perceived quality of the product before the user reaches any functionality.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Read the caption of the sixth field.
Actual result: The caption reads “Confirmez vorte mot de passe”.
Expected result: The caption reads “Confirmez votre mot de passe”.
How to fix: Fix the string and move all interface texts into a localisation dictionary.

Title: The phone format error says the field is required
Description and impact: The format rule carries the text “Ce champ est requis” — “this field is required”. The user sees it with the field filled in and cannot tell what to change. It is a direct consequence of copying the text from the required rule.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Type +33612345678 into the Numéro de téléphone field.
3. Read the error text.
Actual result: “Ce champ est requis” is shown while the field holds a value.
Expected result: The message describes the expected number format.
How to fix: Replace the text with a description of the format, for example “Entrez un numéro à 8–16 chiffres”.

Title: Field values are not trimmed before submission
Description and impact: Leading and trailing spaces are stored as typed. An email copied with a trailing space — the most common paste scenario — is rejected on format instead of being trimmed, and the user cannot see why.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Type a name with spaces at both ends into the first-name field.
2. Paste an email address with a trailing space into the email field.
3. Submit the form and read the stored name value.
Actual result: The name is stored with its spaces. The address with a trailing space is rejected as badly formatted.
Expected result: Values are trimmed before validation and before submission.
How to fix: Apply setValueAs or a shared trim handler to every text field.

Title: The emptiness check lets a whitespace-only string through
Description and impact: The check tests the value for truthiness, and a string of spaces is truthy. A four-space name therefore passes both the client character-set check and the server emptiness check, and lands in the database.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create with "first_name": "    ".
2. Read the stored row.
Actual result: The response is 201 and the database holds a row of spaces.
Expected result: 400: the field is empty once trimmed.
How to fix: Trim the value before checking and compare the resulting length against zero.

Title: A stray asterisk is rendered above the consent checkbox
Description and impact: The field component always renders a caption block with a required asterisk. The checkbox is given no caption, so an empty line with a lone red character remains, attached to nothing.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Look at the area between the confirm-password field and the consent text.
Actual result: A single red asterisk with no caption is displayed between the fields.
Expected result: No stray character appears there.
How to fix: Skip the caption block when no placeholder prop is passed.

Title: The consent checkbox has no error text
Description and impact: The required rule is written as an object with the value true but no message field. The error block renders empty: the user sees that the button does nothing but cannot tell what is missing.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Fill every form field with valid values.
2. Leave the consent checkbox unticked.
3. Inspect the area under the checkbox and the state of the button.
Actual result: The error object exists but its message property is undefined, leaving an empty element under the checkbox.
Expected result: A text explaining that consent is required is shown.
How to fix: Set message on the required rule.

Title: The disabled submit button looks exactly like an enabled one
Description and impact: The button is disabled while the form is invalid, yet keeps the same bright yellow background, full opacity and a working hover effect. The user clicks, nothing happens, and no explanation appears anywhere. Combined with DEF-43 and DEF-45 this produces a form that silently refuses to work.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form without filling anything in.
2. Hover over the S'inscrire button and click it.
3. Compare the computed styles with how the button looks once the form is valid.
Actual result: disabled is true, yet the background rgb(255, 208, 1) and opacity 1 match the enabled state and the hover effect still fires.
Expected result: The disabled state is visible: muted background, changed cursor, no hover effect.
How to fix: Add disabled styles, or keep the button enabled and surface the errors on click.

Title: A password mismatch is not shown when the main field is edited after confirmation
Description and impact: The match rule is evaluated only when the confirmation field changes. If the passwords already matched and the main password is then edited, no error appears, yet the form becomes invalid and the button goes dead. The result is a dead end: no visible errors, and no way to submit.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Type identical passwords into both fields and confirm the button is enabled.
2. Edit the main password field only.
3. Inspect the confirmation field and the state of the button.
Actual result: No error text appears under the confirmation field, while the submit button becomes disabled.
Expected result: “The passwords do not match” appears under the confirmation field.
How to fix: Declare deps on the password field, or call trigger for the confirmation when it changes.

Title: An unknown route renders a completely blank page
Description and impact: The router declares only the root and /success, with no catch-all route. A typo in the address or a stale link produces a white screen with nothing on it and no way back other than editing the URL by hand.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the application.
2. Navigate to /nonexistent-page-404.
3. Inspect the page content and the root element.
Actual result: The page is blank and the root element contains no child nodes.
Expected result: A 404 page with a link back to the form, or a redirect.
How to fix: Add a route with the path * rendering a 404 page.

Title: The thank-you screen opens directly without a registration
Description and impact: The /success route is not guarded by navigation state, so anyone can reach the screen by direct link. This is not a vulnerability, but it is misleading and makes conversion counting by screen views meaningless.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the application in a new tab.
2. Navigate to /success without filling in the form.
Actual result: The “Thank you for subscription!” screen is shown with no prior registration.
Expected result: The user is redirected to the form.
How to fix: Pass a success flag through navigation state and redirect when it is absent.

Title: The password visibility toggle cannot be reached from the keyboard
Description and impact: The icon is a plain block with a click handler: no tabindex, no role, no accessible name. A keyboard-only user can neither focus it, nor activate it, nor learn that it exists. The page offers just eight focusable elements: seven fields and the button.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Tab through the entire form.
3. Try to reveal the typed password without a mouse.
Actual result: The element is a div with no tabindex, role or aria-label, and Tab skips over it.
Expected result: The toggle receives focus and responds to Enter and Space.
How to fix: Replace the block with a button of type button carrying aria-pressed and a text label.

Title: The form fields carry no autocomplete attributes
Description and impact: Not one field has an autocomplete attribute, so the browser and the password manager do not recognise this as a sign-up form. Autofill for name, phone and address never fires and no password suggestion appears. The user types all seven fields by hand.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form in a browser with autofill enabled.
2. Place the cursor in the name field and check whether saved values are offered.
3. Check every field for an autocomplete attribute.
Actual result: The autocomplete attribute is absent on all seven fields and no autofill suggestions appear.
Expected result: The fields carry given-name, family-name, tel, email and new-password.
How to fix: Set the appropriate autocomplete value on each field.

Title: Clicking the consent text does not toggle the checkbox
Description and impact: The terms text sits in its own paragraph beside the field and is not wrapped in a label. Hitting the 16-by-16-pixel checkbox is noticeably harder than hitting the line of text, particularly on a touch screen.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Click the text “J'ai lu et accepté les conditions générales d'utilisation de Wiregate”.
3. Check the state of the checkbox.
Actual result: The checkbox state is unchanged, and the page contains no label elements.
Expected result: Clicking the text toggles the checkbox.
How to fix: Wrap the checkbox and the text in a shared label.

Title: Error messages are not programmatically associated with their fields
Description and impact: The error text is rendered as a plain block after the field, without aria-describedby and without an alert role. A screen reader neither ties the error to the field nor announces its appearance, so a blind user discovers the problem only by returning to the field manually.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form with a screen reader running.
2. Trigger an error in any field.
3. Check the field for aria-describedby and the error block for a role.
Actual result: The fields have no aria-describedby, the error block has no alert role, and the text is never announced.
Expected result: The error is tied to its field and announced when it appears.
How to fix: Give the error block an id, reference it from aria-describedby, and add role="alert".

Title: Required fields are marked with nothing but a red asterisk
Description and impact: Not one field carries the required attribute; the requirement is conveyed visually only. A screen reader reads the asterisk as punctuation or skips it, leaving the user unaware of which fields are mandatory.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Check every field for a required attribute.
3. Listen to the fields with a screen reader.
Actual result: Zero fields carry the required attribute; the requirement is conveyed by colour and a symbol alone.
Expected result: Fields are marked with required or aria-required.
How to fix: Add required to the fields and keep the asterisk as a visual echo.

Title: The email and phone fields are declared as plain text
Description and impact: Both fields use type text instead of email and tel. On a mobile device the standard keyboard opens instead of the numeric and email ones, and the browser's built-in format check never runs. Filling the form on a phone takes noticeably longer.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form on a mobile device or with emulation enabled.
2. Tap the Numéro de téléphone field.
3. Tap the Votre email field.
Actual result: Every text field has type text and the standard alphabetic keyboard opens.
Expected result: The phone field uses type tel and the email field uses type email.
How to fix: Pass the correct type to each field.

Title: The fields carry no maximum-length attribute
Description and impact: Length limits exist only as validation rules, so the user can type or paste any number of characters and learns about the limit from an error message alone. When pasting a long string this reads as a refusal without a reason.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Paste a string longer than 28 characters into the name field.
3. Check the fields for a maxlength attribute.
Actual result: No field carries a maxlength attribute and input is not constrained.
Expected result: Input is capped at the field level, or the excess is trimmed with an explanation.
How to fix: Pass maxLength to the field alongside the validation rule.

Title: The document language is declared as English on a French interface
Description and impact: The markup sets the language attribute to en while the entire interface is in French. A screen reader pronounces French text with English rules, and the browser's built-in translator never offers a translation.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Inspect the lang attribute on the root markup element.
Actual result: lang is set to en while the page content is entirely French.
Expected result: lang is set to fr.
How to fix: Correct the attribute and derive it from the selected locale.

Title: Message texts inside one form are mixed across two languages
Description and impact: Field captions and some messages are French while the remaining error messages are English. Within a single form the user sees both “Ce champ est requis” and “First Name must be at least 4 characters”. For a French-speaking audience half the hints are unreadable.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Trigger an error in the name field.
3. Trigger a format error in the phone field.
4. Compare the languages of the two messages.
Actual result: The name field shows an English message while the phone field shows a French one.
Expected result: Every interface text is in one language.
How to fix: Translate the messages into French and move them into a localisation dictionary.

Title: The tab title and favicon are still the template defaults
Description and impact: The browser tab shows “React App” and the stock create-react-app icon. A user with several tabs open cannot find the right one, and in bookmarks and history the page looks like somebody else's scaffold.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Look at the browser tab title and icon.
Actual result: The title is “React App” and the icon is the create-react-app template logo.
Expected result: The title carries the product name and the icon matches the brand.
How to fix: Replace the title, the favicon and the contents of manifest.json.

Title: The social sign-up component is written but rendered nowhere
Description and impact: The file with the Google and Facebook buttons exists in full, with the Facebook button hard-coded as disabled, yet no screen imports it. Dead code has to be carried through every refactor, and anyone reading the code goes looking for functionality that is not there.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form and look for the Google and Facebook buttons.
2. Count the buttons on the page.
3. Search the project for imports of the SocialMediaFields component.
Actual result: The page holds one button, S'inscrire, and the component is imported nowhere.
Expected result: Either the block is wired into the form, or the file is deleted.
How to fix: Decide on the feature: wire it up or delete the file.

Title: The text for existing users is not a link
Description and impact: The bottom of the form asks “Vous avez déjà un compte?” but offers no sign-in link beside it. A registered user who lands here hits a dead end and has to find the sign-in page on their own.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the form.
2. Scroll to the bottom of the card.
3. Click the text “Vous avez déjà un compte?”.
Actual result: The text is not clickable and the form carries no link to a sign-in page.
Expected result: A sign-in link sits next to the question.
How to fix: Add the link, or remove the text until a sign-in page exists.

Title: The markup uses a font class Tailwind never generates
Description and impact: The class font-OpenSans sits on the form card, but the Tailwind config has no font-family section, so the class is never generated. The typeface comes from a global rule in index.scss alone. The class creates a false impression of controlled typography and would survive any refactor of the global styles unnoticed.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Build the frontend.
2. Search the built stylesheet for font-OpenSans.
3. Check tailwind.config.js for a fontFamily section.
Actual result: font-OpenSans appears zero times in the built CSS and the config has no fontFamily section.
Expected result: The class is declared in the config and sets a font family.
How to fix: Declare the family under theme.extend.fontFamily, or drop the class from the markup.

Title: The response does not match the declared type
Description and impact: The method is declared as returning ShowUserDto with four fields, yet it actually returns the saved entity together with the identifier, the consent flag and any stray fields from the request. An API consumer cannot rely on the declared contract, and the extra fields expose how the store is built.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send a valid POST /users/create.
2. Compare the fields of the response with the ShowUserDto declaration.
Actual result: The response carries id and is_agree on top of the four declared fields.
Expected result: The response contains exactly the fields declared in ShowUserDto.
How to fix: Assemble the response explicitly, or add ClassSerializerInterceptor with @Exclude on the hidden fields.

Title: The responses carry no security headers
Description and impact: There is no content policy, no MIME-sniffing protection, no framing protection and no strict transport requirement. The helmet package is not installed. For a form that accepts passwords this is a baseline that is simply missing.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send any request to the API.
2. Inspect the full list of response headers.
Actual result: Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options and Strict-Transport-Security are all absent.
Expected result: Those headers are present with helmet's default values.
How to fix: Install helmet at the application entry point.

Title: A response header discloses the framework in use
Description and impact: Express adds a header naming the framework by default. That is a hint for automated scanning: knowing the stack narrows the set of vulnerabilities an attacker needs to probe.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send any request to the API.
2. Find the X-Powered-By header in the response.
Actual result: X-Powered-By: Express.
Expected result: The header is absent.
How to fix: Call disable('x-powered-by') on the Express instance, or install helmet.

Title: The internal JSON parser message is returned to the client
Description and impact: A malformed body sends the parser's message, character position included, back to the caller. Harmless in itself, it signals that internal errors are not normalised into a single shape, and something more sensitive could leak later.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create with the body {oops and the header Content-Type: application/json.
2. Read the response body.
Actual result: 400 with the text “Unexpected token o in JSON at position 1”.
Expected result: 400 with a generic malformed-body message.
How to fix: Add an exception filter that normalises parse errors into a single response.

Title: The user record has no timestamps
Description and impact: The table holds six columns and no created or updated marks. Investigating an incident, building a sign-up funnel or spotting traces of the overwrite from DEF-02 is impossible: nothing records when a row appeared or whether it changed.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Start the database.
2. Run \d users and read the column list.
Actual result: The columns are id, first_name, last_name, email, phone_number, password. There is no created_at and no updated_at.
Expected result: The table carries creation and modification timestamps.
How to fix: Add @CreateDateColumn and @UpdateDateColumn and apply them through a migration.

Title: TypeORM is configured to reshape the schema automatically
Description and impact: The synchronize option is on, so the schema is aligned to the entity classes on every start. Renaming a field in code silently drops the column along with its data. In production this is a direct route to data loss without a single migration.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open backend/ormconfig.ts.
2. Find the synchronize option.
Actual result: synchronize: true.
Expected result: synchronize is off and the schema is driven by migrations.
How to fix: Turn the option off and introduce TypeORM migrations.

Title: Failed inserts consume identifier sequence values
Description and impact: Every request that reaches the database and is rejected there still advances the counter. Harmless on its own, it indicates that invalid data passes validation and reaches the storage layer. Under a stream of bad requests the identifiers develop visible gaps.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Empty the table.
2. Send two requests without the first_name field, each answering 500.
3. Create a valid user and check its identifier.
Actual result: The successful record received identifier 5 instead of 3: two values were consumed by rejected inserts.
Expected result: Identifiers run consecutively because invalid requests never reach the database.
How to fix: Reject invalid data in validation before touching the database — see DEF-08.

Title: The request body size is bounded only by the Express default
Description and impact: No application-level limit exists on either layer, so the only boundary is the default hundred-kilobyte body parser. A 92-kilobyte name reaches the database successfully, because the column length is unbounded too.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Send POST /users/create with a first_name of 92 kilobytes.
2. Send the same request at 204 kilobytes.
3. Check the table contents after the first request.
Actual result: 92 kilobytes answers 201 and the row is written. 204 kilobytes answers 413 request entity too large.
Expected result: Both requests are rejected by an application-level length check.
How to fix: Constrain field lengths in the DTO and set an explicit body parser limit.

Title: The lint command silently rewrites source files
Description and impact: The lint script has the auto-fix flag baked in, so the check does not report a problem, it edits the code. The pipeline step will never go red, while the developer sees unexplained changes in the working tree. Along the way it turns out that the committed code does not satisfy its own formatting configuration.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Confirm the working tree is clean.
2. Run yarn lint in the backend directory.
3. Run git status.
Actual result: Four files changed: app.config.ts, user.dto.ts, user.controller.ts, user.service.ts. Linter output: 1 problem (0 errors, 1 warning).
Expected result: The linter reports problems and leaves files untouched.
How to fix: Remove the fix flag from the lint script and add a separate lint:fix script.

Title: The database password is written directly into the run configuration
Description and impact: The value is hard-coded in docker-compose and lands in the repository. Together with DEF-33, which publishes the port, and DEF-03, which stores user passwords in clear text, it completes a full compromise chain.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open docker-compose.yml.
2. Find the POSTGRES_PASSWORD variable.
Actual result: POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "secret" — the password sits in the repository in clear text.
Expected result: The password comes from environment variables or a secret manager.
How to fix: Move the value into .env, add .env to .gitignore and ship a .env.example.

Title: The backend starts without waiting for the database to be ready
Description and impact: The database service has no readiness probe and the dependency is declared without a condition, so the backend container counts as started the moment the Postgres process launches. On a cold machine the backend can reach for the database before it accepts connections and crash. The defect reproduces intermittently, which makes it unpleasant to debug.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Remove the local images and volumes so the start is cold.
2. Run docker compose up.
3. Read the backend container log for connection errors.
Actual result: The database container has no health check and the dependency is declared without a condition.
Expected result: The backend starts only once the database is accepting connections.
How to fix: Add a healthcheck on pg_isready and set condition: service_healthy in depends_on.

Title: Dependencies are installed into the mounted directory as root
Description and impact: The containers run as root and install dependencies straight into the project source directory on the host. The node_modules directories, around a gigabyte in total, are owned by root, so a developer cannot delete or modify them without elevated rights. Build output is also mixed in with the sources.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Start the stack with the README command.
2. Wait for the dependency installation to finish.
3. Run ls -ld backend/node_modules on the host.
Actual result: The directories are owned by root:root and total about one gigabyte inside the source tree.
Expected result: The files belong to the user who started the stack, or the dependencies live in a named volume.
How to fix: Set user to the current user's id, or move node_modules into a dedicated volume.

Title: The compose file uses an obsolete version key
Description and impact: The version key is ignored by Compose v2 and produces a warning on every run. Noise in the output trains people to skip warnings, and something important eventually gets lost among them.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Run docker compose up.
2. Read the first lines of output.
Actual result: Warning: “the attribute `version` is obsolete, it will be ignored”.
Expected result: The output is clean, with no warnings.
How to fix: Delete the version line from docker-compose.yml.

Title: The frontend runs in development mode
Description and impact: The configuration launches the development server, meaning no minification, source maps included and debugging tooling active. The demo stand does not reflect what a user would see: bundle size, load speed and error behaviour all differ from a production build.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open docker-compose.yml and inspect the frontend service command.
2. Open the application and check for source maps in the developer tools.
Actual result: react-scripts start is used — a development server with source maps and no minification.
Expected result: A production build is produced and served as static files for the demo.
How to fix: Add a separate service or build stage that serves the output of react-scripts build.

Title: Ownership of the email address is never confirmed
Description and impact: The account is created immediately and no confirmation email is sent. Someone else's address can be registered, and together with DEF-09, which permits duplicates, and DEF-22, which imposes no rate limit, the database quickly fills with records for addresses their owners do not control.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Register an address that is knowingly not yours.
2. Check whether a row appeared in the table.
3. Check whether a confirmation email is sent.
Actual result: The record is created at once and no confirmation is requested.
Expected result: The account stays inactive until the link in the email is followed.
How to fix: Introduce address confirmation through a one-time link and store a confirmed flag on the record.

Title: Email validation lets through domains that cannot exist
Description and impact: The expression permits a domain beginning with a hyphen and an address with a bracketed IP literal. Both are meaningless in an ordinary consumer form and mean the address was mistyped, which the user discovers only by never receiving an email.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Type a@-b.co into the email field.
2. Type a@[127.0.0.1].
3. Send the same values to the API.
Actual result: Both values are accepted by the form and by the server, answering 201.
Expected result: Both values are rejected as malformed.
How to fix: Use a vetted email validation library instead of a hand-written expression.

Title: The environment variables are documented nowhere
Description and impact: The repository holds neither a sample environment file nor a README section, although the application reads six variables. Deploying outside Docker or pointing the app at another database requires reading the variable names out of docker-compose and the sources.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Clone the repository.
2. Look for a .env.example file.
3. Read the README for a description of the environment variables.
Actual result: There is no sample file, and the README contains only the start command with no variable documentation.
Expected result: The repository ships a .env.example listing every variable and its purpose.
How to fix: Add .env.example and an environment section to the README.

Title: The password travels between the frontend and the API unencrypted
Description and impact: The API address uses the http scheme, so the password crosses the network in clear text. On a local machine this is harmless, but nothing in the default configuration prevents the same stand from being deployed beyond localhost as is.
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open docker-compose.yml and inspect the REACT_APP_API_URL value.
2. Submit the form and check the request scheme in the network panel.
Actual result: The address is http://localhost:8000 and the request carrying the password goes over http.
Expected result: The exchange runs over https, with local development explicitly carved out.
How to fix: Configure TLS for non-local environments and enable strict transport through helmet.
